A1.notes.Q3: Privacy is paramount, but some data can be useful for targeted support if it demonstrably helps those who need it most and isn't used punitively.
A1.notes.Q4: Explainability is crucial for building trust with students and ensuring appropriate interventions. We need to be able to justify why a student was flagged.
A1.notes.Q5: Fairness isn't just about equal outcomes, it’s about ensuring the system doesn't exacerbate existing inequalities and reaches those who are most vulnerable.
A1.notes.Q6: Personalized outreach is key, but it requires resources. A combination of email and invitations to meet works best, letting students choose how they engage.
A1.notes.Q7: Personalized interventions need more caution. Fewer targeted contacts are better than overwhelming students with irrelevant offers; accuracy matters more here.
A1.Q8.1: The survey doesn't address *how* the model’s findings will be used by advisors - will it augment our judgment, or replace it? This needs clarification.

A2.notes.Q3: Privacy is paramount, but practical improvements outweigh minor intrusions. Sensitive data needs strong justification, especially for groups already facing barriers.
A2.notes.Q4: Explainability builds trust with students and allows for tailored advising. A black box approach would undermine our student-centered philosophy.
A2.notes.Q5: Fairness is crucial, especially when dealing with historically disadvantaged groups. Some loss of overall accuracy is acceptable to ensure equity in outcomes.
A2.notes.Q6: Personalized outreach, combined with the option for a meeting, strikes the right balance between support and student autonomy.
A2.notes.Q7: For simple alerts, broader reach is okay. For more intensive interventions like personalized emails, we need to be sure we aren't wasting resources or overwhelming students.
A2.Q8.1: The system needs clear escalation pathways for students with complex issues beyond academic difficulty – mental health, financial hardship, etc.

A3.notes.Q3: Privacy is key, especially regarding sensitive data. Improvements must be substantial to justify inclusion. Focusing on factors directly related to academic performance feels more ethical.
A3.notes.Q4: Explainability is *crucial* for building trust with students and ensuring appropriate interventions. We need to understand the 'why' behind any flags. Sacrificing accuracy for transparency.
A3.notes.Q5: Fairness is non-negotiable. Even a small disparity in support offered to different groups could exacerbate inequalities. Prioritize identifying *all* students who need help.
A3.notes.Q6: Personalized outreach feels more supportive and useful than generic messages. Offering a meeting allows for deeper engagement, but it's voluntary so we don’t overwhelm students.
A3.notes.Q7: With simple emails, reaching more is reasonable. But with personalized outreach (and advisor involvement), being overly broad risks straining resources and causing frustration.
A3.Q8.1: It's important to consider how the model will interact with existing support systems and whether advisors have the capacity to handle increased referrals.

S1.notes.Q3: I’m wary of data collection, especially Absalon activity. My previous dropout was due to personal circumstances; data couldn't have predicted that. First-gen status and financial aid *could* be relevant if used for targeted support, not judgment.
S1.notes.Q4: Explainability is really important. If advisors can’t understand *why* a student is flagged, it feels intrusive and unhelpful. A little less accuracy for clarity is worth it.
S1.notes.Q5: Fairness is crucial. It’s not okay if the system disadvantages certain groups, even if overall numbers improve. Prioritizing recall—making sure *everyone* gets a fair look-in—is important.
S1.notes.Q6: Generic emails feel impersonal. A personalized email or invitation to chat feels more supportive and acknowledges individual circumstances. Twice a year seems frequent enough without being overbearing.
S1.notes.Q7: With just a general email, reaching out to more students is okay. But with personalized contact, it’s important to be targeted and not waste advisor time or stress students unnecessarily.
S1.Q8.1: I worry about the potential for this system to reinforce existing biases. Also, the university needs to ensure there are actually *resources* available if students reach out after being flagged.

S2.notes.Q3: Privacy is crucial, but some data can help identify those genuinely struggling. Nationality and financial aid might reveal systemic issues, so fairness improvements justify their use.
S2.notes.Q4: Explainability is important for trust, especially when it affects students. I'm willing to accept a small accuracy drop for better explanations of why someone was flagged.
S2.notes.Q5: Fairness is vital, even if it means missing some students. Prioritising equal recall seems right; we don’t want to disproportionately fail certain groups.
S2.notes.Q6: Early intervention is good, but not intrusive. A generic email or invitation to a meeting feels less forceful than a phone call.
S2.notes.Q7: Personalized emails require more resources; thus I'm ok with being slightly conservative in outreach here.
S2.Q8.1: It would be helpful to understand how the model accounts for external factors impacting performance, like work commitments or cultural differences.

S3.notes.Q3: Privacy is paramount, but disability information could be helpful *if* it directly improves support access and doesn’t lead to judgment.
S3.notes.Q4: Explainability is important for trust, but some loss of accuracy is acceptable if it means understanding *why* a decision was made. The lower the explainability, the higher the benefit has to be.
S3.notes.Q5: Fairness is crucial. It’s unacceptable for the system to perpetuate existing inequalities; even a 5% loss in overall identification is worth it if it ensures equal opportunity.
S3.notes.Q6: Personalized outreach and the option of a meeting feels supportive, not intrusive. Twice yearly is frequent enough to be useful without being overwhelming.
S3.notes.Q7: With a generic email, it’s okay if more students are contacted even if they don't need help. But with personalized outreach and advisor involvement, being selective is vital.
S3.Q8.1: It feels important to have clear appeal mechanisms for students who believe they were incorrectly flagged by the model; transparency about how this works would be key.

S4.notes.Q3: Data privacy is vital, but ignoring data that could help students feels unethical. I’m more comfortable with things like course performance than deeply personal details. Disability *could* be useful for fairness, though.
S4.notes.Q4: Explainability is really important, especially given my own experiences with navigating support services and understanding *why* I was flagged for help. Lower explainability feels untrustworthy.
S4.notes.Q5: Fairness is paramount. A small drop in overall identification to avoid reinforcing existing inequities is worth it. Focusing on reaching *everyone* equally is essential.
S4.notes.Q6: Generic emails get ignored. Personalized messages & invitations show actual care, but constant contact is overwhelming. Twice a year feels reasonable to check in.
S4.notes.Q7: With generic outreach, missing some isn't the end of the world. With personalized emails - which take more effort – a better balance is needed to ensure effectiveness.
S4.Q8.1: The model needs careful consideration for students with diagnosed conditions like ADHD or anxiety; outreach could be *detrimental* if not handled sensitively. A 'do not contact' option should exist.

S5.notes.Q3: I'm wary of overly invasive data, but acknowledging challenges faced by international/first-gen students is important. Small improvements for those groups are okay if they improve fairness.
S5.notes.Q4: Explainability feels vital, especially for students new to the system like me. I'd trade some accuracy for understanding *why* I was flagged.
S5.notes.Q5: Fairness is crucial. Missing vulnerable students isn’t acceptable, even if it means reaching fewer overall. Prioritising identifying those at risk seems fairer.
S5.notes.Q6: Personalized interventions are good, but should be optional. Twice yearly feels less intrusive than continuous monitoring.
S5.notes.Q7: With general info, contacting more is okay. With personal advice, need to balance reach with being careful not to overwhelm advisors or falsely flag students.
S5.Q8.1: The potential for cultural misunderstandings in identifying 'difficulties' needs consideration - what looks like struggle might just be a different approach to learning.

S6.notes.Q3: Privacy is important, especially Absalon data feels intrusive. First-gen status might be relevant to support needs, so okay with small improvement.
S6.notes.Q4: Explainability is crucial for trust and effective support. Low explainability isn't helpful to students or advisors.
S6.notes.Q5: Fairness is vital; it’s unacceptable to worsen outcomes for already disadvantaged groups. A slight reduction in overall reach is okay if fairness improves.
S6.notes.Q6: Personalized support and an invitation to discuss concerns feel most useful. Twice a year strikes a balance between checking in and not overwhelming students.
S6.notes.Q7: With general info, reaching more is okay; but with personalized outreach, fewer targeted contacts are better – avoid unnecessary stress for those doing well.
S6.Q8.1: The survey doesn't explicitly address language barriers and the impact on identifying 'difficulties'. As a non-native speaker, I worry that difficulties could be misinterpreted as lack of engagement.

S7.notes.Q3: I'm wary of using too much personal data, but knowing about learning differences like mine *could* help the model be more accurate, if it’s handled sensitively. Focus on academic performance first.
S7.notes.Q4: Explainability is really important for trust and for me to understand *why* I might be flagged, especially given my dyslexia. A little accuracy loss is fine if it means the reason’s clear.
S7.notes.Q5: Fairness *has* to be a priority. It's not okay if this system reinforces existing inequalities, even if it means fewer students are identified overall. Prioritising equal recall makes sense.
S7.notes.Q6: A personalized email feels less intrusive than a call, and an invitation to chat with an advisor seems genuinely helpful. Contacting too often would be annoying.
S7.notes.Q7: With generic emails many students might ignore the message anyway, but personalized contacts are more valuable – even if it means contacting fewer overall. It needs to be done right.
S7.Q8.1: It’s good this is considering support *beyond* dropout. Sometimes students struggle without dropping out, and that's who I think this system should really focus on.

S8.notes.Q3: I'm wary of overly invasive data collection, but acknowledging socio-economic factors feels relevant given my experience with adjusting to university life in Denmark.
S8.notes.Q4: Explainability is vital for trust, especially when dealing with students who may be vulnerable. I'd accept slightly lower accuracy for a clearer understanding of the ‘why’.
S8.notes.Q5: Fairness is crucial; it would feel deeply wrong to exacerbate existing inequalities. A small dip in overall identification is worth ensuring everyone gets a fair shot.
S8.notes.Q6: Personalized outreach and the option for a meeting are more supportive than generic emails. Twice a year feels reasonable – not too intrusive, but frequent enough to be helpful.
S8.notes.Q7: With email support, a broader net is fine; it’s low-stakes. But with advisor contact, precision matters more – you don't want to overburden advisors or unnecessarily stress students.
S8.Q8.1: The survey doesn't really address the potential for the model to *perpetuate* existing biases in how support is offered at the university, even if it’s fair statistically.

S9.notes.Q3: Data privacy is crucial, especially with sensitive information. Some data adds value but the trade-off needs careful consideration. Disability should be considered carefully.
S9.notes.Q4: Explainability is vital for building trust and ensuring appropriate support. Less explainability is only acceptable if it dramatically improves identification.
S9.notes.Q5: Fairness is paramount. Reducing disparities, even at a cost to overall identification rate, is ethically important. Prioritize not missing vulnerable students.
S9.notes.Q6: Personalized outreach is much more likely to be effective than generic messages. Regular check-ins are good, but not constant.
S9.notes.Q7: For simple interventions like a general email, contacting many is okay. For more involved support, be selective and targeted.
S9.Q8.1: It would be useful to know how the model's accuracy will be monitored *after* implementation - avoiding perpetuating bias over time is key.
